title: Module inputs dependency graph and safety playbook
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a proposal and playbook for simplifying and stabilizing Terraform module inputs/outputs across VPC, IAM, and cluster (EKS/GKE/AKS) primitives. Goal is to reduce accidental coupling, make upgrades nonbreaking, and provide a repeatable verification and migration path for consumers (internal teams and customer on-prem kits).

Background and motivation:
- Over the past 18 months we accumulated many small variations of the same primitives: vpc-module-v1 (lots of outputs), vpc-shared-mode, eks-cluster-basic, eks-cluster-for-privdep. Consumers keep copying bits of outputs into downstream modules, creating brittle implicit dependencies.
- Upgrades are risky: renaming outputs or changing output shape breaks consumer state or requires manual mapping. We need a clear contract surface and a safety playbook for making changes.

Design principles (non-negotiable):
1) Keep module API minimal: inputs and outputs should support common use cases, prefer optional extension points rather than many variants.
2) Names must be stable and explicit: avoid environment-prefixed keys (do not expose aws_vpc_id_for_xyz). Use neutral canonical names (vpc_id, private_subnet_ids, public_subnet_ids).
3) Do not return provider-internal opaque objects as outputs (e.g., full aws_subnet resources). Only return primitive scalar values and lists of scalars.
4) Avoid bifurcation: a single module should not both create and import the same resource under different flags. Prefer a create/import boolean with well-documented behavior and outputs that are always present (may be empty lists).
5) Provide a lightweight compatibility shim: every major refactor must include aliased outputs for at least one release cycle.

Recommended canonical output surface (starter list) - VPC primitive:
- vpc_id (string)
- cidr_block (string)
- private_subnet_ids (list(string)) - ordered by AZ when possible
- public_subnet_ids (list(string))
- isolated_subnet_ids (list(string)) - for on-prem segmentation if relevant
- route_table_ids (map(string)) - keys: public|private|isolated -> id
- nat_gateway_ids (list(string)) - may be empty
- dns_zone_id (string) - optional if we edge into private-dns behavior

IAM primitive outputs (minimal):
- role_arns (map(string)) - named roles created by module, e.g., {"eks_node": "arn:...", "controllers": "arn:..."}
- policy_arns (map(string)) - reusable managed policies
- instance_profile_ids (map(string)) - if used for nodes or on-prem proxies

Cluster primitive outputs (EKS/GKE/AKS) - common surface: 
- cluster_name (string)
- cluster_endpoint (string)
- cluster_ca_certificate (string, base64)
- kubeconfig_template (string) - optional, templated kubeconfig with placeholders for credentials
- node_group_ids (map(string))
- load_balancer_sg_id (string) - security group for LB or ingress
- cluster_autoscaler_role_arn (string)

Variable naming conventions and types (examples):
- <component>_enabled (bool) e.g., eks_enabled: toggles resource creation vs import mode.
- <component>_create_mode (string, one of [create, import, external]) for finer control
- <resource>_ids (list(string)) for lists, <resource>_id (string) for singletons
- map inputs use maps of strings when referencing other module outputs: e.g., node_group_config = map(string) where keys are logical names
- Avoid nested object types where possible. If necessary, use map(string) with predictable JSON-coded values as fallback to maintain compatibility with older Terraform versions.

Dependency graph guidance (how consumers should wire modules):
- Principle: Consumers should rely only on the canonical scalar outputs above. Do not do: data.aws_subnet_ids directly in consuming modules based on provider-specific lookup.
- Provide example wiring: vpc -> iam and vpc -> eks. EKS should accept vpc_id and private_subnet_ids as explicit inputs and not call data sources.
- Where multiple pieces of info are needed together (e.g., subnet id + route table mapping), prefer passing both explicitly rather than relying on discoverability.

Backward compatibility & upgrade playbook (step-by-step):
1) Deprecation announcement: add deprecation warning to README and module outputs for renamed fields.
2) Add aliases: keep old output names in place, mark them as deprecated in docs and output descriptions. Implementation: add new output and duplicate value to old name for one release.
3) Add conversion helpers: small helper locals module consumers can call to normalize between old and new shapes. Publish example usage in README.
4) Release cadence: keep aliases for at least 2 minor releases (approx 8 weeks) after announce.
5) Remove old outputs in major release only. Before removal: run internal impact analysis and reach out to teams with direct consumption (use state scanning, see below).

Automated safety checks we must run for all refactors:
- Static usage scan: search repo for direct references to module outputs by path and by name across internal repos. Produce list of potentially affected consumers.
- Terraform plan smoke tests: for a representative set of consumer stacks (we keep a small test matrix per major customer and internal product), run terraform plan against both old and new module versions in a parallel workspace to detect diffs in state references.
- Integration scenario tests: boot ephemeral test stacks in a sandbox org: create vpc -> eks -> demo-app and run end-to-end smoke tests (kubeconfig works, pods schedule, LB attaches).
- State import tests: for import mode changes, validate that existing resources can be imported with no drift.

Migration checklist for a module change (PR template):
- [ ] Why? short summary of the user-visible change.
- [ ] Impact analysis: list of repos & stacks found by static scan.
- [ ] Backwards compatibility plan (aliasing, deprecation period).
- [ ] Automated tests added: unit + integration test entries.
- [ ] README updated with migration example and sample terraform code.
- [ ] Rollout plan (which teams to notify and rollout windows).

Examples: renaming public_subnets -> public_subnet_ids
- Implementation: add new output public_subnet_ids = module.vpc.public_subnets (or split/join if needed), keep old public_subnets = public_subnet_ids for two releases. Add description: "DEPRECATED: use public_subnet_ids - will be removed in v2.0".
- Consumer recommendation: switch to public_subnet_ids, add a small local in consumers/main.tf to normalise until old output is removed.

State scanning heuristic (how we find consumers):
- Grep for module.<module_name>.<output_name> across all infra repos (including forks and legacy scripts).
- Additionally scan pre-generated terraform plans stored in CI artifacts (we store plan.json for prod rollouts).
- For ambiguous matches, open low-friction tickets to the owning repo to confirm usage.

On-prem considerations (airgapped / restricted environments):
- Modules must offer an explicit import path: if we rely on external DNS or KMS, provide configuration to create placeholder local resources or accept externally provided IDs.
- Reduce reliance on dynamic data lookups (metadata endpoints, cloud provider APIs) where possible; explicit inputs preferred.
- Provide local test harness: a small dockerized tool that validates module output surface and produces a "compatibility manifest" that downstream tooling can read offline.

Testing matrix suggestions (minimal):
- TF version compatibility: 1.1, 1.5, latest 1.x (note object type handling differs).
- Providers: aws (current), gcp (for GKE), azure (for AKS) - verify outputs are provider-agnostic when possible or clearly namespaced.
- Feature flags: create_mode toggled, node_pool rolling update test, iam role change test.

Operational playbook for a breaking change (emergency rollback):
- If a change breaks consumer stacks in CI: 1) Immediately revert module to previous released version in registry and create hotfix tag. 2) If state drift occurred, coordinate with affected teams to run the state correction script (we maintain a small set of idempotent remediation TFs) 3) Postmortem: capture root cause, why static scan missed; improve heuristics.

Documenting outputs and embellished descriptions:
- Each output must include: description, example value, stability (stable|experimental|deprecated), since_version.
- Use examples directory with a short snippet showing how a consumer should reference the output.

Conventions for multi-cloud primitives: 
- Prefix cloud-specific outputs with provider when the shape diverges, e.g., gcp_subnetwork_self_link vs aws_subnet_ids. Try to keep the generic name (subnet_ids) when equivalent semantics exist; otherwise create provider-specific outputs.

Open questions for the team (items to decide in follow-up sync):
- Do we enforce a strict semantic version policy for modules in registry (major.minor.patch) tied to breaking output changes? Proposal: yes, require major bump for output renames or removals.
- How long should aliasing be guaranteed? Proposal: 2 minor releases minimum.
- Do we publish a machine-readable compatibility manifest with each release (recommended)?

Next actions (short-term):
- Owners: Aisha to draft a module API styleguide from these notes and publish to Confluence (by 2025-01-31).
- Engineering work: Riley to implement the static usage scanner as a lightweight GH Action (P0 for Q1).
- Tests: Sofia to enumerate the consumer test matrix and add two representative stacks to the sandbox pool.

Appendix: quick example snippets (consumer best-practice)
1) Importing vpc outputs into eks module:
module "vpc" {
  source = "git::ssh://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//vpc?ref=v1.3.0"
}
module "eks" {
  source = "git::ssh://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//eks?ref=v2.0.0"
  cluster_name = "prod-uswest"
  vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id
  private_subnet_ids = module.vpc.private_subnet_ids
}
2) Migration local shim example (consumer):
locals {
  public_subnet_ids = try(module.vpc.public_subnet_ids, module.vpc.public_subnets)
}

Notes on ergonomics: keep examples tiny and copy-pastable. Document should evolve into a living Confluence page with a short checklist for module authors and a PR template we can attach to the repo.

End of note.
